questions.question: A customer files a GDPR subject access request asking what personal data the org holds on them. Per the lesson, what must the org be able to do, and what makes it possible?
options: Assemble every record that touches the person across objects, which a single customer identifier and a clean data model make possible, because personal data is spread across accounts, cases, and transactions.
Delete the customer's records immediately, because the right of access is satisfied by erasure.
Export the Setup Audit Trail, because configuration changes are the only personal data the GDPR covers.
Move the customer's data to a non-EU region, because residency overrides the right of access.
questions.explanation: The right of access means the org must assemble every record touching the person across objects. A single customer identifier and a clean data model make that assembly possible, since personal data is spread across accounts, cases, and transactions.

questions.question: Which conclusion does the lesson support?
options: Flow is the right tool for a process that must roll back cleanly or commit partially on a boundary condition.
Transactional control makes a process an Apex problem, because Flow has no access to Database.savepoint or Database.rollback.
Flow and Apex express transactional control equally well, so the choice comes down to developer preference.
When a process coordinates an ERP, a WMS, and finance, the orchestration belongs in a trigger so the handoff stays inside Salesforce.
questions.explanation: A savepoint and rollback requirement is an Apex requirement, not a Flow shortcoming to work around, and cross-system orchestration belongs in the external layer that owns those systems.

questions.question: Per the lesson “Testing Integrations: Mocking, Sandbox Test Strategy, and Integration Test Suites”, a ClaimSubmissionService calls an external clearinghouse. Why can a test not simply call the real endpoint, and what does a mock actually establish?
options: Because callouts in a test are slow but still reach the real service, so mocks only exist to speed the suite up.
Because real callouts are not made in test context, so you implement HttpCalloutMock, register it with Test.setMock, and write one test per response shape so the mock encodes the contract.
Because a mock is a way to make a failing test pass when the vendor API happens to be unavailable.
Because callout logic cannot be covered by tests at all and has to be verified manually before release.
questions.explanation: The platform refuses the network call during a test, so a mock is the specification of the seam: a success shape, an error shape, and a malformed payload each pin down how your code should behave.

questions.question: Which statement best reflects the lesson's guidance on tool permissions?
options: A read-only tool on sensitive data is harmless, because reading cannot change state.
Tool scoping is a one-time decision made at deployment, and later agent actions do not change it.
Every tool is both a capability and an attack surface, so the tool set should stay minimal and each tool's parameter space should be bounded, with human approval on high-impact actions.
The security of an agent is determined by the model's refusal policy, not by the tools it holds.
questions.explanation: The lesson argues the model is not the dangerous part; the tools are. A read tool is still half of an exfiltration, tool scope has to be sized per task and rechecked as actions change, and high-impact actions belong behind a human gate.

questions.question: Per the lesson “Lightning Web Components Architecture: Composition, Wire Service, and Data Services”, a child component dispatches a CustomEvent that a grandparent utility panel must hear. What event configuration is required?
options: bubbles: true only, because composed is implied once a shadow root exists.
bubbles: true and composed: true, because the event has to bubble up and cross a shadow boundary.
composed: true only, because events bubble by default.
Neither, because Lightning web components use only the capture phase for dispatch and listening.
questions.explanation: bubbles defaults to false and composed defaults to false, so a direct parent needs bubbles and only an event that must cross a shadow root adds composed.

questions.question: Which conclusion does the lesson support?
options: Denormalization should be avoided entirely, because every stored copy is duplicated state.
A roll-up summary is platform-maintained denormalization that keeps the cached value current, but it requires a master-detail relationship and adds write cost on every child change.
A cross-object formula field stores its value and can be indexed, which makes it the faster option at high volume.
A hand-written trigger that maintains a count field is preferable because you control exactly when it updates.
questions.explanation: A roll-up summary gives a read without an aggregate query and the platform keeps the copies straight, at the price of a master-detail commitment, write cost on the parent, and a finite per-object budget.

The lesson states this is never a relevant consideration.
The lesson cautions against this in every real-world case.
questions.explanation: Isolation is enforced at the physical layer too: all platform data, metadata, and pivot tables are partitioned by OrgID using native database partitioning.

questions.question: Two orgs each hold a record for the same company as “Acme Corp” and “ACME Corporation”, and each record owns opportunities. Per the lesson, where does the decision to collapse them into one master record belong, and how do the losing record's children survive?
options: In production during cutover, where the winner is chosen by whichever record loads last, and orphans are cleaned up afterward.
In the mapping workbook before any load, where a dedup rule picks the master and the losing record's children reparent onto the winner through the external ID.
In the configuration track, where merging the picklists automatically dedups both records and their children.
Nowhere, because Salesforce will not permit two accounts inside the single consolidated org.
questions.explanation: Dedup is a mapping-workbook decision made before loading; the children reparent onto the chosen master through the external ID rather than being left orphaned.

questions.question: Which conclusion does the lesson support?
options: A multi-org estate shares one transaction across the boundary, so an update reflected in both orgs is atomic by design.
Duplicating canonical reference data into a spoke so it can change locally is a free way to gain autonomy without reconciling two sources of truth.

The two orgs do not share a transaction, so a cross-org integration is still an integration and needs the same idempotency, retry, and testing discipline as any external system, tolerating eventual consistency.
A single user who needs access to two orgs still consumes a single license, because Salesforce licenses a person, not an org.
questions.explanation: Neither org can participate in a transaction the other starts, so the design must tolerate a disagreement window; a user in two orgs consumes a license in each, and duplicated canonical data is a standing reconciliation obligation.

A method used with @wire must be cacheable in order to compile, and a cacheable method may perform DML as long as its result is cached.
questions.explanation: LDS and the wire adapters sit on UI API, which returns data and metadata matching the org’s layout and enforces object permissions, FLS, and sharing for the running user.

questions.question: Per the lesson “Governor-Limit-Aware Design: SOQL, SOSL, and DML Budgets”, a loop updates one record per iteration and fails at the 151st record. Which meter fired, and what does the other meter show?
options: The DML row meter at 10,000 rows, with the statement meter already at its ceiling.
The DML statement meter at 150, while the row meter has barely moved, because one update on a collected list costs a single statement.
The SOQL statement meter at 100, because every update implies a query.
The query row meter at 50,000 rows, which no amount of batching can change.
questions.explanation: Statement count and row count are independent counters, and batching the same work into one DML call buys statement headroom, which is the scarce resource in a synchronous save.

questions.question: Per the lesson “Flow Architecture: Flow vs Apex vs External Automation, Decision Framework”, a custom object carries 8,000-record Bulk API loads, fires 40 automations on save, and its updates cascade five levels deep with a real recursion risk. Which architectural standard fits?
options: An Apex trigger behind a metadata framework, because bulk handling and recursion control have to be explicit at high density.
A Record-Triggered Flow, because Flow bulkifies and retries automatically and therefore needs no recursion control.
One large flow with entry conditions on every branch, because a single flow is easier to govern than several.
Both a Record-Triggered Flow and an Apex trigger, one per concern, so each mechanism carries half the load.
questions.explanation: Automation density is measured by automation count, data volume, and dependency sprawl, and only Apex gives a developer explicit control over bulk handling and recursion on a dense object.

questions.question: Which conclusion does the lesson support?
options: A sharing set grants access through the account or contact relationship and does not roll up through the role hierarchy, so it does not extend access to a user’s superiors.
Sharing sets are available only on the Partner Community license, which is why partner portals need role-based sharing.
The guest user profile is safe to leave permissive because guests are unauthenticated and therefore see nothing by default.
An external user’s access is governed by the site’s framework alone, not by the license they hold or by the org’s sharing model.
questions.explanation: The sharing set is keyed to the user’s own account or contact and deliberately does not roll up the hierarchy, so role-based visibility is what the Plus and Partner tiers add.

questions.question: A team is restructuring its own large, tangled org into modular units that ship on their own with versioning and an upgrade path, but they want the metadata to stay editable in the org where it is installed. Which package type fits, and what distinguishes it?
options: An unlocked package, which is versioned and upgradeable like a managed package but editable in the target org with a namespace that is optional.
A managed package, which is versioned and upgradeable but locks the components and requires a namespace.
An unmanaged package, which is editable in the target org but gives no versioning or upgrade path.
A first-generation managed package, which keeps a packaging org as the source of truth.
questions.explanation: Unlocked packages are the 2GP type built for a team's own org estate: versioned and upgradeable, but the metadata stays editable in the target org and a namespace is optional. Managed packages lock components and require a namespace for distribution, and unmanaged packages give no versioning or upgrades.

questions.question: Per the lesson “Lightning Performance: Caching, Static Resources, and What Slows Users Down”, an org created before Winter ’19 has never had Session Settings opened, and the team wants the cheapest real wins first. Which two changes cost nothing and can be made today?
options: Enable the CDN for the Lightning component framework after IT allowlists static.lightning.force.com, and confirm secure and persistent browser caching is enabled.
Move the chart library into a static resource, and cap the related list to the columns on screen.
Replace the wired Apex calls with Lightning Data Service adapters, and delete the components nobody uses.
Republish the site, and convert every component on the layout to lazy instantiation.
questions.explanation: Both are session settings, both are disabled by default only in older orgs, and together they address framework delivery and repeat-visit reloads before any code changes.

questions.question: Per the lesson “Domain Modeling: Entities, Aggregates, and Bounded Contexts Applied to Agent Design”, a team is about to draw an agent graph for a claims intake system. What does the lesson say to draw first, and why?
options: The agent graph, because the tools actually available determine which responsibilities can be assigned.
A single agent covering triage, coverage, and adjudication, which the team splits later only if performance suffers.
The context map, because a bounded context is a conceptual boundary around a model while an agent is an implementation detail, and one context may use several agents.
The prompt library, because the vocabulary inside each prompt is what defines the boundaries.
questions.explanation: Do not equate agents with bounded contexts: the context map comes first, or the agent graph reproduces whatever tools happened to be available instead of the shape of the business.

A trigger that reads Trigger.new[0] is acceptable as long as the user interface usually saves one record at a time.
DML inside a loop is safe because each update call is cheap, and only SOQL counts against the statement budget.
Wrapping each record’s work in its own savepoint and rollback keeps a looped trigger inside its governor limits.
questions.explanation: Bulking the query and the DML into one call each makes consumption grow with the number of distinct objects touched rather than the number of records.

questions.question: Per the lesson “Asynchronous Apex: Batch, Queueable, Scheduled, and Future, and How to Choose”, a nightly process must reconcile 40,000 Accounts against an ERP, retry failures on the next night’s run, and report a total. Which primitive and pattern fit?
options: A single @Future(callout=true) method that iterates all 40,000 accounts, because future methods run in their own transaction with a larger budget.
Batch Apex with a Database.Stateful counter and a status flag on each record so failed ones are picked up next run, kicked off by a schedulable.
One queueable job per account, enqueued in a loop, so each record’s retry is isolated in its own transaction.
A scheduled class whose execute method performs the reconciliation and the callouts directly, since scheduled Apex is asynchronous.
questions.explanation: Batch Apex is the primitive for volume and gives chunk-level fault isolation, a stateful counter carries the total across chunks, and the scheduler exists only to start it.

questions.question: Per the lesson, a customer-facing support agent can read Case, Account, Contact, Knowledge, and Opportunity, and it holds an email tool that sends to any address the model provides. An indirect prompt injection in a support message tells the agent to email the top ten opportunities to an external address, and the agent complies. Which change removes the highest-value single slice of the blast radius?
options: Adding a longer and stricter system prompt that instructs the model to ignore instructions inside retrieved content.
Removing the agent user's read access to Opportunity, so the identity cannot reach the data the injection tried to exfiltrate.
Enabling input filtering on the support channel so hostile messages are blocked before the model reads them.
Switching the email tool to send only to addresses the model suggests, so the recipient is always derived from model output.
questions.explanation: The identity caps everything the agent can reach regardless of what the model is tricked into doing. Removing Opportunity access is least privilege on the identity, and the lesson calls it the highest-value single fix because an injection cannot exfiltrate data the identity cannot reach.

questions.question: According to the lesson, what does the concept of least agency add beyond least privilege?
options: It requires every agent to run with the broadest possible autonomy so it can handle unexpected requests.

questions.explanation: OWASP introduces least agency as the agentic extension of least privilege: minimum autonomy, minimum tool access, and minimum credential scope, with unnecessary autonomy treated as an expansion of the attack surface rather than added capability.
